newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-Rebels control Zaire Gecamines - Tenke head.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Rebels control Zaire Gecamines - Tenke head.

text.p: Rebel forces control Zaire's main cobalt producer Gecamines and are in the process of establishing their authority over the body, Brian Spratley, head of the Zaire-based Tenke Fungurume Project said on Wednesday.

"The (rebel) Kabila government has effectively taken control of all the assets of Gecamines and I suppose that they are trying to establish some sort of legal proprietorship over Gecamines, in which case it impacts on our joint venture," Spratley, who left the rebel-held city of Lubumbashi in southern Zaire on Saturday, told Reuters.
"As far as we know, Gecamines is at a standstill at the moment, their offices are closed. I have no information as to what they are doing at their various sites," Spratley said.

Spratley said his firm had held discussions with Laurent Kabila's rebel movement to establish that legal and constitutional contract arrangements and concessions made under Zaire law would be honoured by the new regional government.
"We believe they will honour the agreement," Spratley said.
Tenke Fungurume Project is a subsidiary of Toronto-listed Tenke Mining Corp.
Tenke Mining is developing a vast copper/cobalt mine in the mineral-rich Shaba province of Zaire and signed a deal with Zaire's government last December.
Spratley was speaking prior to a conference organised by the Cobalt Development Institute in Hong Kong.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) has snatched half of Zaire from Kinshasa since taking up arms last October.
"Frankly, if the democratic alliance wants to establish authority over Gecamines, they must presumably reconstitute the board of Gecamines," Spratley said.
He said it was not clear how Kabila's government would proceed.
Trading from Gecamines may have stopped until lines of authority were clarified, Spratley said.

"Until the (Kabila) government has established for themselves how these trades are going on and (how) the revenue from these trades is going to go to Gecamines, I think they may have stopped it," he said.
A senior African industry source said on Monday that Zaire's next cobalt shipment would take place next week and that mining facilities had not been damaged.
Spratley said there was a perception that cobalt availability was short.
"The cobalt price will depend on stocks held by consumers, stocks held by traders and some stocks held by producers," Spratley said.
The price would return to normal after perceptions changed, he said, adding that the actual physical situation had not changed drastically.
Cobalt prices have jumped over the past few months as Zaire's rebel forces advanced.
"As far as I know, the new alliance government is trying to get everything back moving as quickly as possible," Spratley said.
"I think that everything is really back to normal and the outside investors that we met are working normally again," he said.
The Tenke-Fungurume project, the first major foreign investment in Zaire since the 1970s, is a joint venture with Gecamines.
